reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Classic lesions are well-demarcated, salmon-pink plaques with adherent silvery scale, favouring extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp, and the lumbosacral region
Gentle removal of scale may reveal pinpoint bleeding points (Auspitz sign), and new plaques can appear at sites of trauma (Koebner phenomenon)
Nail changes such as pitting, onycholysis, and oil-drop discolouration are common and support the diagnosis
Up to a third of patients develop psoriatic arthritis, so ask about joint pain, stiffness, and dactylitis at every review
Recognise clinical variants: guttate (often post-streptococcal in younger patients), inverse/flexural, pustular, and erythrodermic forms

Treatment is stepped: topical agents (corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues) for limited disease, phototherapy for widespread involvement, and systemic or biologic immunomodulators for severe or refractory disease
Screen for and address associated cardiometabolic risk, obesity, and depression, as psoriasis is a systemic inflammatory condition
Avoid abrupt withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids, which can precipitate a pustular or erythrodermic flare
reference.pathophysiology: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated disorder driven by dysregulated activation of the innate and adaptive immune systems, particularly the interleukin-23/T-helper-17 axis and tumour necrosis factor signalling. Activated T cells and dendritic cells release cytokines that drive keratinocyte hyperproliferation and abnormal differentiation, dramatically shortening epidermal turnover time and producing thickened, scaly plaques. Dilated dermal vessels and a neutrophilic and lymphocytic infiltrate account for the erythema and, in pustular variants, sterile collections of neutrophils. A strong polygenic predisposition (including PSORS1/HLA-C associations) interacts with triggers such as infection, trauma, drugs, and stress.
additionalDifferentials: Seborrhoeic dermatitis (especially on the scalp and face)
Chronic eczema or lichen simplex chronicus
Secondary syphilis in atypical guttate-like eruptions
additionalInvestigations: Largely a clinical diagnosis; skin biopsy reserved for atypical presentations
Throat swab or streptococcal serology when guttate psoriasis is suspected
Joint assessment and imaging when psoriatic arthritis is suspected
Baseline and monitoring bloods (including liver function and infection screening) before systemic or biologic therapy
Metabolic screening for cardiovascular risk factors, lipids, and glucose
redFlags: Erythroderma with widespread redness, scaling, and impaired thermoregulation requiring urgent care
Generalised pustular psoriasis with fever and systemic upset
Rapidly progressive joint destruction or dactylitis suggesting aggressive psoriatic arthritis
Signs of secondary infection or sepsis in extensive skin breakdown
reference.prognosis: Psoriasis is a lifelong relapsing-remitting condition; most patients achieve good control with appropriate therapy, but disease severity fluctuates and associated arthritis and cardiometabolic disease influence long-term outcomes.
pitfalls: Mislabelling scalp or flexural psoriasis as seborrhoeic dermatitis or fungal infection
Overlooking psoriatic arthritis until irreversible joint damage has occurred
Using potent topical steroids in flexures or on the face without appropriate caution
Precipitating pustular or erythrodermic flares by withdrawing systemic corticosteroids
management: Topical corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues and their combinations, with emollients and coal tar or salicylic acid, for limited plaque disease
Phototherapy with narrowband UVB or psoralen-UVA for extensive or refractory plaque and guttate disease
Conventional systemic agents such as methotrexate, ciclosporin or acitretin for moderate-to-severe disease
Biologic and targeted therapy directed at tumour necrosis factor, interleukin-17 and the interleukin-12/23 axis, or oral apremilast, for severe or refractory disease
Actively screen for and treat psoriatic arthritis, and manage cardiometabolic comorbidities including lipids, glucose, weight and smoking
Identify and address triggers such as streptococcal infection in guttate disease, culprit drugs, skin trauma and stress
Baseline and ongoing monitoring bloods with infection screening, including latent tuberculosis, before and during systemic or biologic therapy
Urgent inpatient management and dermatology referral for erythrodermic or generalised pustular psoriasis
